requirement_summary: The service must get the applicant's full name.
The service must get the applicant's address.
The service must get the applicant's date of birth.
The service must get details of the applicant's health, backed by a medical report.
The service must get details of every other adult in the household.
The service must get details of the applicant's children, wherever they live, and any other children in the household.
The service must get details of the applicant's accommodation.
The service must find out the outcome of any earlier application to foster by the applicant or anyone in their household.
The service must find out the outcome of any earlier application to adopt by the applicant or anyone in their household.
The service must find out the outcome of any application to register as a childminder or other early or later years provider.
If the applicant was approved by another fostering service in the last 12 months, the service must get its name and address.
The applicant must give the names and addresses of 2 people who will give personal references.
The applicant and every household member aged 18 or over need an enhanced criminal record certificate with children's barred list information.
The service must get details of the applicant's current marriage, civil partnership or similar relationship.
The service must get details of any previous marriage, civil partnership or similar relationship.
If the applicant fostered for another service in the last 12 months, the service must ask that service for a written reference.
The service must interview at least 2 people the applicant names as referees and write up each interview.
The service must consult the council where the applicant lives and take its views into account.
With the applicant's consent, the service may ask another fostering service that approved them for its records.
With the applicant's consent, the service may ask an adoption agency that approved them for its records.
No one can be approved if they, or an adult in the household, were convicted or cautioned for a specified offence as an adult.
The service must get details of the applicant's personality.
The service must cover the applicant's religion and their capacity to care for a child of any religion.
The service must cover racial origin, cultural and language background, and capacity to care for a child of any background.
The service must cover the applicant's past and present work or occupation.
The service must cover the applicant's standard of living.
The service must cover the applicant's leisure activities and interests.
The service must cover any experience of caring for the applicant's own and other children.
The service must cover the skills, competence and potential that bear on caring well for a placed child.
The service must also get any other information it thinks relevant. Motivation to foster is not named in the English schedule.
The service must judge whether the applicant is suitable to foster and whether the household is suitable for any child.
The written report must include the service's proposals for any terms of approval.
The law approves individuals, but 2 people who will share the care of a child should be assessed jointly.
legal_citation: DfE statutory guidance, Assessment and approval of foster carers (July 2013), p 9

requirement_summary: A service may decide not to assess if the applicant's offer does not fit the children it is recruiting for.
legal_citation: DfE statutory guidance, Assessment and approval of foster carers (July 2013), p 6

requirement_summary: The registration of interest form should at least ask for the name and address of the people applying.
The registration of interest form should ask for permission to start the Stage One checks.
The registration of interest form should confirm the person has not registered interest with another agency.
The registration of interest form should ask when the agency can contact the person in the following week.
The registration of interest form should include questions that check the person meets the eligibility rules for adopting.
The minimum age to adopt is 21. There is no upper age limit, and agencies must not turn people away because of age.
Agencies must not refuse a registration of interest because of, for example, ethnicity, age, health, sexual orientation or religious beliefs.
The agency must get an enhanced criminal record certificate with children's barred list information for the applicant and each adult in the household.
The agency cannot find someone suitable if they, or an adult household member, have a specified conviction or caution from adulthood.
The agency must get the applicant's name.
The agency must record the applicant's sex.
The agency must get the applicant's date and place of birth.
The agency must get the applicant's address, including the council area.
If a married person or civil partner applies alone, the agency must record why.
The agency must get details of any earlier family court proceedings involving the applicant.
The applicant must name 3 referees. No more than 1 of them may be a relative.
The agency must get the name and address of the applicant's doctor (GP).
The agency must get the date and place of any marriage or civil partnership, or details of a partner relationship.
The agency must get details of any previous marriage, civil partnership or relationship.
The agency must record whether the applicant is domiciled or habitually resident in the British Islands, and for how long.
The agency must get details of other household members, including the applicant's children wherever they live.
The agency must get a doctor's written report on the applicant's health after a full examination.
The health report must give the applicant's weight and height.
The health report must include a family health history, including serious illness and hereditary conditions.
The health report must cover infertility, or the reasons for deciding not to have children, where this applies.
The health report must cover past health, including serious physical or mental illness, disability, accidents and hospital care.
The health report must cover obstetric history, where this applies.
The health report must cover any present illness, its treatment and outlook.
The health report must cover worrying alcohol use, smoking and use of habit-forming drugs.
The agency must get a written report of each interview with the applicant's referees.
Where it thinks it necessary, the agency must get a reference from a former spouse, civil partner or partner.
The agency must ask the council where the applicant lives for any relevant information, and get a written report if there is some.
A modified version of the process applies to approved foster carers and to people who have adopted before.
With consent, the agency may ask a fostering service for its records about an applicant who is an approved foster carer.
The agency must get a photograph and physical description of the applicant.
The agency must cover the applicant's racial origin and cultural and language background.
The agency must cover the applicant's religion.
The agency must record the applicant's relationship to the child, if there is one.
The agency must describe the applicant's personality and interests.
The agency must get a family tree of the applicant, their brothers and sisters and their children, with ages.
The agency must get a chronology of the applicant's life from birth.
The agency must record how the applicant's own experience of being parented has influenced them.
The agency must cover any experience of caring for children, and assess the applicant's ability.
The agency must cover how the applicant and others in the household are likely to relate to a placed child.
The agency must describe the wider family and its likely role for the applicant and a placed child.
The agency must cover the applicant's home and neighbourhood.
The agency must cover the local community, including friendships and social networks.
The agency must cover education history and how it has influenced the applicant.
The agency must cover employment history and how it has influenced the applicant.
The agency must cover current employment and the applicant's views on balancing work and childcare.
The agency must get details of the applicant's income and spending.
The agency must cover capacity to meet a child's needs, share their history and support them through loss and trauma.
The agency must record the applicant's reasons for wanting to adopt.
The agency must record views on adoption, parenting, parental responsibility, home life, education, religious and cultural upbringing, and contact.
The agency must record what other household members and the wider family think about the adoption.
The report must include a summary of the applicant's health written by the agency's medical adviser.
For a couple, the agency must have proper regard to how stable and lasting their relationship is.
The agency should discuss interest in fostering for adoption and note any interest in the report.
legal_citation: DfE statutory guidance, Adoption (July 2013), para 3.55 and 3.56
